summary: Discovery focused on partition tolerance, multi-region routing options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), SLAs and expected failure modes. Customer wants deterministic failover behavior for critical inference endpoints and clarifications on auditability + private deployment requirements.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-03 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Redwood SA), Maya Chen (Calypso CTO), Liam O'Neill (Platform), Rita Shah (SecOps), Omar Reyes (SRE)

[00:00] Jordan Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining us. quick intro — i'm jordan, AE at Redwood. priya and samir here from the engineering side. maya, would you like to kick off with a bit of context about where you are and the main reliability concerns?

[00:18] Maya Chen: yeah thanks jordan. so um Calypso is rolling out an internal inference layer for our clinical decision support features. we have a few latency-sensitive endpoints that must stay online even during region loss. high level question is, can redwood give us deterministic fallback + audit logs for those failovers, and what are the tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated and private for our requirements.

[00:42] Priya Patel: great, thanks. when you say deterministic fallback, do you mean a hard policy like always fail to a replica in eu-west then to on-prem, or a more fluid policy that prefers lower cost but falls back to other variants?

[00:58] Liam O'Neill: we need predictable behavior. for clinical endpoints if us-east goes down, traffic should fail over to eu-west within, ideally, 15s for synchroneous calls. for long running batch stuff we're more flexible. also need full audit trail for each request: who, model version, which region served it.

[01:23] Samir Rao: noted. that maps to two different SLOs: hotpath inference (low-latency, strict failover) and background jobs. for the hotpath we often recommend Dedicated with multi-region peering or Redwood Hosted with explicit region pinning plus canary fallbacks. can i ask about your data residency constraints?

[01:42] Rita Shah: all patient PII must stay in EU for EU patients. US patient data may be handled in US. we need key management with customer KMS for private deploys and audit logs retained for seven years. SOC2 and ISO are required.

[01:58] Jordan Kim: we support KMS integrations for Private and Dedicated; Hosted can be configured with customer-managed keys in some cases but there are limitations depending on region and cloud provider. i'll send the security packet after the call with exact details.

[02:15] Maya Chen: how do you handle split brain scenarios? if the private control plane loses connectivity to a region, what happens to in-flight requests and KV cache consistency?

[02:30] Priya Patel: good question. our runtime is not a distributed consensus database; we treat model state (KV cache) as ephemeral per instance. for in-flight requests we have graceful degradation: if KV cache isn't reachable we replay from model weights which increases latency but keeps correctness. for cache inconsistency between regions we do eventual reconciliation and we recommend routing policies that avoid simultaneous writes across regions for mutable state.

[02:58] Omar Reyes: so that means during a region partition we might get higher latency or some tokenier — how much slower are we talking? we need numbers for SLO calculations.

[03:12] Priya Patel: it depends on model size and quantization. for a 70B model on p4 equivalent, a cache miss adds about 20-120ms per token on average. for smaller models it's less. i'll put concrete numbers in the benchmark report.

[03:28] Liam O'Neill: we also run an offline reranking pipeline that uses embeddings. if a region is out, can requests be routed to a cheaper region temporarily, or do you force a fail block?

[03:40] Samir Rao: routing is policy-driven. you can define hard rules (must be eu-west), soft rules (prefer us-east but allow eu fallback up to X ms) and tiered fallbacks (hosted -> dedicated -> private). you can also attach cost thresholds to limit fallback to high-cost regions.

[03:59] Maya Chen: this tiered fallback sounds useful. can you explain how in practice we test it before we commit? we want to run chaos drills that simulate region blackholes and measure end-to-end behavior including audit logs.

[04:16] Priya Patel: we do two things: 1) synthetic failover test — we simulate regional loss at the routing layer and observe how requests move through policies, and 2) live workload replay — we replay recorded traffic through different routing knobs to measure latency and error budgets. both can be automated in a 48-72 hour run.

[04:33] Rita Shah: on audit logs, we need tamper-evidence and per-request entries that show model id, model sha, route decision, and token counts. does redwood's hosted product expose all that?

[04:45] Jordan Kim: yes hosted exposes detailed traces and token-level cost breakdowns, but for tamper-evidence we recommend Dedicated or Private where logs can be exported to your SIEM and signed by your KMS. we'll include sample log schema in the security packet.

[05:02] Liam O'Neill: what about fallback to model variants? for example, default to a quantized model during outages to reduce latency and preserve throughput. can routing do model-substitutions?

[05:14] Priya Patel: absolutely. our routing supports model compatibility sets and automatic substitution — e.g., a 70B fp16 can fallback to a 70B quantized or a smaller 13B model depending on policy. we also support KV cache warming so a substituted model can warm caches from a read-only prefix cache where appropriate. note: quality regressions must be tested via prompt sets.

[05:37] Maya Chen: quality regressions are a big concern. we'll need guardrails so that critical endpoints never fallback to a variant that fails a set of validation prompts. can this be tied into the routing policy?

[05:49] Samir Rao: yes, you can annotate routes with evaluation gates — a route only allows substitution if the candidate model passes the configured evals. that's part of Redwood Optimize integration; it's on by default in Dedicated and Private pilots if you want.

[06:04] Omar Reyes: on multi-region replication: do you replicate model artifacts synchronously? our infra team is sensitive to egress costs and storage duplication.

[06:16] Priya Patel: we replicate artifacts asynchronously across regions. initial sync will copy weights; thereafter we do delta transfers where possible. artifact storage and transfer costs are visible in the dedicated pricing examples we'll share. also note private on-prem deployment can avoid cross-region egress entirely by pre-staging artifacts.

[06:35] Maya Chen: timeline question — if we do a pilot, what's realistic for a minimal pilot with dedicated nodes in two regions and a private control plane in our VPC?

[06:47] Jordan Kim: typically 4-6 weeks for dedicated with two regions if cloud accounts and network peering are configured quickly. private control plane adds another 2-3 weeks depending on your networking and KMS setup. Priya, does that match?

[06:58] Priya Patel: yes. also lead time for hardware or reserved GPU capacity can extend that, but we can start with hosted region pinning for an initial week of testing while dedicated capacity is reserved.

[07:12] Liam O'Neill: curious about traffic split during failover. do you do connection draining or immediate cutover? we want to avoid duplicate side-effects to downstream services.

[07:24] Samir Rao: by default we do connection draining with a configurable grace window. for idempotent calls you can allow immediate reroute, but for non-idempotent calls we recommend retry middleware with dedupe tokens. Redwood integrates with commonly used request-id headers to support dedupe.

[07:40] Rita Shah: ok, that helps. one more sec on encryption: we need HSM-backed signing for long-term logs. you said dedicated/private supports KMS — HSM options?

[07:51] Jordan Kim: yes, Private supports HSM via partner KMS/HSM integrations; Dedicated supports customer-managed keys in certain clouds. i'll include exact cloud-by-cloud capabilities in the packet.

[08:04] Maya Chen: can you walk us through a hypothetical outage scenario? like us-east has a regional outage, traffic should move to eu-west, token costs should be attributed correctly, logs must show model substitution, and post-mortem artifacts must be generated.

[08:20] Priya Patel: sure — example flow: 1) router health checks detect node loss in us-east; 2) router marks region as degraded and applies the first fallback policy (eu-west for clinical endpoints); 3) in-flight requests are drained for X seconds, new requests are routed to eu-west; 4) if the eu-west variant is quantized we attach a substitution tag in the trace and route only if eval passes; 5) all decisions are logged to the audit stream and exported to your SIEM; 6) we generate an incident bundle with traces and request-level metrics for the post-mortem.

[09:02] Omar Reyes: who owns the runbook? we want clear ops steps to take during an incident — do you provide a starter playbook?

[09:12] Samir Rao: yes, we provide an ops playbook template that covers detection, routing knobs, rollback steps, and mitigation actions. we can customize and co-author it during the pilot.

[09:22] Maya Chen: budget constraints: what's the unit economics for maintaining hotpath in two regions vs single region plus fallback? we need cost vs availability tradeoffs presented to finance.

[09:34] Jordan Kim: we'll model that in the pricing sheet. high level: dual hotpath is more expensive but reduces failover time and avoids cross-region latencies; tiered fallback saves cost but increases failover risk. we have case studies we can share.

[09:48] Liam O'Neill: a few quick technical things for the pilot scope doc: we will provide target RPS per endpoint, the prompt set for quality gates, and a list of critical downstream services. we'll also want a 72-hour chaos window where redwood simulates region loss.

[10:05] Jordan Kim: perfect. next steps recap — priya to run the failover benchmark, jordan will send security packet and pricing, maya to supply RPS and endpoints, then we'll schedule the pilot kickoff. anything else?

[10:20] Maya Chen: one last ask — can you include an example of the log schema and the exact event names for routing decisions so our SIEM mapping is straightforward?

[10:30] Jordan Kim: yes will include.

[10:34] Rita Shah: thanks all.

[10:36] Jordan Kim: thanks everyone, i'll follow up with calendar invite for the pilot kickoff and the documents.

End of meeting.
